title: Constrained Stochastic Spectral Preconditioning Converges for Nonconvex Objectives
claim: The method is a forward-then-backward step across dual and primal spaces, and its nonlinear preconditioner matches practice better than the ideal sign.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; geometric diagram beside a function-fit plot
description: The left panel is a cartoon of dual and primal spaces. An orange-to-yellow gradient ellipse labeled "Dual space" holds a point d^k. A dashed black arrow labeled ∇φ*(·) curves down from d^k to a cyan sphere labeled "Primal space". On the sphere, a blue "forward" arrow runs from x^k to an off-sphere point y^k. A short red "backward" arrow then returns from y^k to x^{k+1} on the sphere's surface. The right panel is a line plot of d from 0 to 0.01 against output from 0 to 1. A solid blue 7-step Polar Express curve and a dashed orange d/(ε^4+|d|^4)^{1/4} curve almost overlap. Both rise steeply and saturate at 1. A dotted green sign(d) curve jumps straight to 1. Captions (a) and (b) sit below the panels.
caption: (a) Diagram of the proximal preconditioned gradient method as described in [ref]. The forward step applies a nonlinear preconditioner $\nabla \phi^*$ to the dual space direction $d^k$ (e.g., the gradient $\nabla f(x^k)$) to compute the forward step $y^k$ in the primal space. Since this might leave the constraint set $C$, a backward step is performed to compute $x^{k+1}$. (b) The Polar Express [ref] fits more closely to $\frac{d}{(\varepsilon^4 + |d|^4)^{1/4}}$ with $\varepsilon=3\times 10^{-4}$ than to the actual sign, showing that our theory more faithfully captures the practical implementations of Muon.
abstract: In this work, we develop proximal preconditioned gradient methods with a focus on spectral gradient methods providing a proximal extension to the Muon and Scion optimizers. We introduce a family of stochastic algorithms that can handle a wide variety of convex and nonconvex constraints and study its convergence under heavy-tailed noise, through a novel analysis tailored to the geometry of the proposed methods. We further propose a variance-reduced version, which achieves faster convergence under standard noise assumptions. Finally, we show that the polynomial iterations used in Muon are more accurately captured by a nonlinear preconditioner than by the ideal matrix sign, leading to a convergence analysis that more faithfully reflects practical implementations.
